::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Integrate $\int \frac{\sin x}{\sqrt{3-\cos^4x}} \mathrm{d}x$](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2546024/integrate-int-frac-sin-x-sqrt3-cos4x-mathrmdx), asked by [J.Low](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/508160/j-low) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-12-01; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> $$\int \frac{\sin x}{\sqrt{3-\cos^4x}} \mathrm{d}x$$
>
> I tried the substitution $u=tg(\frac{x}{2}) \implies \mathrm{d}x=\frac{2\mathrm{d}u}{1+u^2}$, which gives
>
> $$\int \frac{\sin x}{\sqrt{3-\cos^4x}} \mathrm{d}x=\int \frac{\frac{2u}{1+u^2}}{\sqrt{3-\frac{1-u^2}{1+u^2}}} \cdot\frac{2\mathrm{d}u}{1+u^2}=\int \frac{u}{\sqrt{3-\frac{1-u^2}{1+u^2}}} \mathrm{d}u=$$
>
> then Substitute $t=\sqrt{3-\frac{1-u^2}{1+u^2}} \implies du=\frac{2\sqrt{3-\frac{1-u^2}{1+u^2}}}{\frac{2u}{ut^2+1}-\frac{2u(u^2-1)}{(u^2+1)^2}}dt$
>
> $$=2\int \frac{1}{t^4-8t^2+16}dt$$
>
> Should I continue or this is wrong? 
>
> Thanks
:::

The good Doctor is correct.  The substitution $u=\cos x$ leads to 
$$\int \frac{\sin x}{\sqrt{3-\cos^4 x}} = - \int \frac{du}{\sqrt{3-u^4}}$$
However, the antiderivative on the right is not an elementary function.  [Wolfram Alpha says][1]
$$-\int \frac{du}{\sqrt{3-u^4}} = -\frac{1}{3^{1/4}} F\left(\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{u}{3^{1/4}}\right) \mid -1 \right)$$
where $F$ is an elliptic integral of the first kind.


  [1]: http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=integrate%20-1%2Fsqrt(3-u%5E4)
